advisory: Structural-only pre-1955 projection, not a complete 1920 Missal corpus. Every unstated formulary is served mechanically from roman-1962 without target-recension collation and must be described as inherited and uncollated rather than complete for 1920.

A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Read at printed pp. 138-142 = leaves n175-n179. The book's Missal section does not reprint this sequence: printed p. 244 directs `For Stabat Mater dolorosa, see page 138.`, and p. 138 heads it `Friday after Passion-Sunday. FEAST OF THE SEVEN DOLOURS OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. VESPERS.` with the incipit `Stabat Mater dolorosa.`, continued under `MATINS (The same continued.)` at p. 140 and `LAUDS (The same continued.)` at p. 141. The three hours together carry the twenty strophes of the Missal sequence with no doxology added at any break, and the last stanza renders both `Christe, cum sit hinc exire` and `Quando corpus morietur`, which is the Missal's ending and not the Breviary hymn's. Ten stanzas against twenty strophes, two for one. The Missal's closing `Amen.` is not rendered.

translations.text:
At the Cross her station keeping,
Stood the mournful Mother weeping,
Close to Jesus to the last:
Through her heart, his sorrow sharing,
All his bitter anguish bearing,
Now at length the sword had pass’d.

Oh, how sad and sore distress’d
Was that Mother highly blest
Of the sole-begotten One!
Christ above in torment hangs;
She beneath beholds the pangs
Of her dying glorious Son.

Is there one who would not weep,
Whelm’d in miseries so deep
Christ’s dear Mother to behold?
Can the human heart refrain
From partaking in her pain,
In that Mother’s pain untold?

Bruis’d, derided, curs’d, defil’d,
She beheld her tender Child
All with bloody scourges rent;
For the sins of his own nation,
Saw Him hang in desolation,
Till his Spirit forth He sent.

O thou Mother! fount of love!
Touch my spirit from above,
Make my heart with thine accord:
Make me feel as thou hast felt;
Make my soul to glow and melt
With the love of Christ my Lord.

Holy Mother! pierce me through;
In my heart each wound renew
Of my Saviour crucified:
Let me share with thee His pain,
Who for all my sins was slain,
Who for me in torments died.

Let me mingle tears with thee,
Mourning Him who mourn’d for me,
All the days that I may live:
By the Cross with thee to stay;
There with thee to weep and pray;
Is all I ask of thee to give.

Virgin of all virgins best!
Listen to my fond request:
Let me share thy grief divine;
Let me, to my latest breath,
In my body bear the death
Of that dying Son of thine.

Wounded with his every wound,
Steep my soul till it hath swoon’d
In his very blood away;
Be to me, O Virgin, nigh,
Lest in flames I burn and die,
In his awful Judgment day.

Christ, when Thou shalt call me hence,
Be thy Mother my defence,
Be thy Cross my victory;
While my body here decays,
May my soul thy goodness praise,
Safe in Paradise with Thee.

Two pointers reach this text. Leaf n617, printed p. 609, heads 30 June `XXX. COMMEMORATION of St. PAUL.` and rubricates `All as on January 25, p. 543`; leaf n552, printed p. 544, then prints for 25 January `Of St. PETER, Deus, qui beato, as on the Feast of his Chair at Rome, the 18th of January, p. 538.` The oration itself stands on leaf n546, printed p. 538, with the Latin cue `Deus, qui beato.` The 1962 index reprints the same three orations under 01-25 and 06-30, and this file already records them at comm-s-petri-apostoli; the English is therefore recorded twice, as at the three commemorations named in the 1962 open_collation_items. translations.caution:
A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across all five and Irons as
an alternative for the Dies irae; it does not argue that either voice is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.

Read at printed pp. 241-244 = leaves n278-n281, under `Sequence, Mass for the Dead.` and the incipit `Dies irae dies illa.` Nineteen stanzas against the Missal's nineteen strophes, one for one; the closing `Amen.` is not rendered. This corrected the recovered lane brief and the then-current guidance row, which had misidentified the London edition's contents. The London 1849 prints it, in its Missal section, between the Lauda Sion and the cross-reference to the Stabat Mater. An independent English of this sequence is therefore not needed for coverage; the alternative Irons text below is offered as a choice of voice, not as a gap-filler. The existing untranslated row for this slot refuses the 1861 witness's own English as a verse paraphrase in the manner of Roscommon; that refusal stands and is not disturbed by this row, which comes from a different book.

translations.text:
Nigher still, and still more nigh
Draws the Day of Prophecy,
Doom’d to melt the earth and sky.

Oh, what trembling there shall be,
When the world its Judge shall see,
Coming in dread majesty!

Hark! the trump, with thrilling tone,
From sepulchral regions lone,
Summons all before the throne:

Time and Death it doth appal,
To see the buried ages all
Rise to answer at the call.

Now the books are open spread;
Now the writing must be read,
Which condemns the quick and dead:

Now, before the Judge severe
Hidden things must all appear;
Nought can pass unpunish’d here.

What shall guilty I then plead?
Who for me will intercede,
When the Saints shall comfort need?

King of dreadful Majesty!
Who dost freely justify!
Fount of Pity, save Thou me!

Recollect, O Love divine!
’Twas for this lost sheep of thine
Thou thy glory didst resign:

Satest wearied seeking me;
Sufferedst upon the Tree:
Let not vain thy labour be.

Judge of Justice, hear my prayer!
Spare me, Lord, in mercy spare!
Ere the Reckoning-day appear.

Lo! thy gracious face I seek;
Shame and grief are on my cheek;
Sighs and tears my sorrow speak.

Thou didst Mary’s guilt forgive;
Didst the dying thief receive;
Hence doth hope within me live.

Worthless are my prayers, I know;
Yet, oh, cause me not to go
Into everlasting woe.

Sever’d from the guilty band,
Make me with thy sheep to stand,
Placing me on thy right hand.

When the curs’d in anguish flee
Into flames of misery;
With the Blest then call Thou me.

Suppliant in the dust I lie;
My heart a cinder, crush’d and dry;
Help me, Lord, when death is nigh!

Full of tears, and full of dread,
Is the day that wakes the dead,
Calling all, with solemn blast,
From the ashes of the past.

Lord of mercy! Jesu blest!
Grant the Faithful light and rest.

translations.text:
Day of Wrath! O day of mourning!
See fulfill’d the prophets’ warning!
Heav’n and earth in ashes burning!
Oh, what fear man’s bosom rendeth
When from Heav’n the Judge descendeth,
On Whose sentence all dependeth!

Wondrous sound the trumpet flingeth,
Through earth’s sepulchres it ringeth,
All before the Throne it bringeth.
Death is struck, and nature quaking,
All creation is awaking,
To its Judge an answer making.

Lo! the Book exactly worded,
Wherein all hath been recorded;
Thence shall judgment be awarded.
When the Judge His seat attaineth,
And each hidden deed arraigneth,
Nothing unavenged remaineth.

What shall I, frail man, be pleading,
Who for me be interceding,
When the just are mercy needing?
King of Majesty tremendous,
Who dost free salvation send us,
Fount of pity, then befriend us!

Think, good Jesu, my salvation
Caused Thy wondrous Incarnation;
Leave me not to reprobation.
Faint and weary Thou hast sought me,
On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me?

Righteous Judge! for sin’s pollution
Grant Thy gift of absolution,
Ere that day of retribution.
Guilty, now I pour my moaning,
All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant groaning.

Thou the sinful woman savedst;
Thou the dying thief forgavest;
And to me a hope vouchsafest.
Worthless are my prayers and sighing;
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
Rescue me from fires undying.

With Thy favour’d sheep O place me,
Nor among the goats abase me,
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
While the wicked are confounded,
Doom’d to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me with Thy Saints surrounded.

Low I kneel, with heart submission,
See, like ashes, my contrition;
Help me in my last condition.

Ah! that day of tears and mourning!
From the dust of earth returning
Man for judgment must prepare him:
Spare, O God, in mercy spare him!
Lord, all-pitying, Jesu Blest,
Grant them Thine eternal rest.
Amen.

translations.text:
Nigher still, and still more nigh
Draws the Day of Prophecy,
Doom’d to melt the earth and sky.

Oh, what trembling there shall be,
When the world its Judge shall see,
Coming in dread majesty!

Hark! the trump, with thrilling tone,
From sepulchral regions lone,
Summons all before the throne:

Time and Death it doth appal,
To see the buried ages all
Rise to answer at the call.

Now the books are open spread;
Now the writing must be read,
Which condemns the quick and dead:

Now, before the Judge severe
Hidden things must all appear;
Nought can pass unpunish’d here.

What shall guilty I then plead?
Who for me will intercede,
When the Saints shall comfort need?

King of dreadful Majesty!
Who dost freely justify!
Fount of Pity, save Thou me!

Recollect, O Love divine!
’Twas for this lost sheep of thine
Thou thy glory didst resign:

Satest wearied seeking me;
Sufferedst upon the Tree:
Let not vain thy labour be.

Judge of Justice, hear my prayer!
Spare me, Lord, in mercy spare!
Ere the Reckoning-day appear.

Lo! thy gracious face I seek;
Shame and grief are on my cheek;
Sighs and tears my sorrow speak.

Thou didst Mary’s guilt forgive;
Didst the dying thief receive;
Hence doth hope within me live.

Worthless are my prayers, I know;
Yet, oh, cause me not to go
Into everlasting woe.

Sever’d from the guilty band,
Make me with thy sheep to stand,
Placing me on thy right hand.

When the curs’d in anguish flee
Into flames of misery;
With the Blest then call Thou me.

Suppliant in the dust I lie;
My heart a cinder, crush’d and dry;
Help me, Lord, when death is nigh!

Full of tears, and full of dread,
Is the day that wakes the dead,
Calling all, with solemn blast,
From the ashes of the past.

Lord of mercy! Jesu blest!
Grant the Faithful light and rest.

translations.text:
Day of Wrath! O day of mourning!
See fulfill’d the prophets’ warning!
Heav’n and earth in ashes burning!
Oh, what fear man’s bosom rendeth
When from Heav’n the Judge descendeth,
On Whose sentence all dependeth!

Wondrous sound the trumpet flingeth,
Through earth’s sepulchres it ringeth,
All before the Throne it bringeth.
Death is struck, and nature quaking,
All creation is awaking,
To its Judge an answer making.

Lo! the Book exactly worded,
Wherein all hath been recorded;
Thence shall judgment be awarded.
When the Judge His seat attaineth,
And each hidden deed arraigneth,
Nothing unavenged remaineth.

What shall I, frail man, be pleading,
Who for me be interceding,
When the just are mercy needing?
King of Majesty tremendous,
Who dost free salvation send us,
Fount of pity, then befriend us!

Think, good Jesu, my salvation
Caused Thy wondrous Incarnation;
Leave me not to reprobation.
Faint and weary Thou hast sought me,
On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me?

Righteous Judge! for sin’s pollution
Grant Thy gift of absolution,
Ere that day of retribution.
Guilty, now I pour my moaning,
All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant groaning.

Thou the sinful woman savedst;
Thou the dying thief forgavest;
And to me a hope vouchsafest.
Worthless are my prayers and sighing;
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
Rescue me from fires undying.

With Thy favour’d sheep O place me,
Nor among the goats abase me,
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
While the wicked are confounded,
Doom’d to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me with Thy Saints surrounded.

Low I kneel, with heart submission,
See, like ashes, my contrition;
Help me in my last condition.

Ah! that day of tears and mourning!
From the dust of earth returning
Man for judgment must prepare him:
Spare, O God, in mercy spare him!
Lord, all-pitying, Jesu Blest,
Grant them Thine eternal rest.
Amen.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

Leaf n696, printed p. 688, heads 2 November `II. COMMEM. of the FAITHFUL, departed.` and rubricates `All as in the Mass (Requiem) p. 510. except the Collect, Fidelium, with its Secret and P. COMM, as in the Common Mass. p. 518, and what follows.` The oration stands on leaf n526, printed p. 518, in `The COMMON MASS for the DEAD`, under the sub-heading `For all the Faithful departed.` with the Latin cue `Fidelium.` The conclusion is printed `Who livest.` The 1861 is a pre-1915 printing and keeps one Mass on 2 November, not three; the `For all the Faithful departed` set it points at is the 1962 First Mass's three orations word for word, which is why this row names that form. translations.text:
Nigher still, and still more nigh
Draws the Day of Prophecy,
Doom’d to melt the earth and sky.

Oh, what trembling there shall be,
When the world its Judge shall see,
Coming in dread majesty!

Hark! the trump, with thrilling tone,
From sepulchral regions lone,
Summons all before the throne:

Time and Death it doth appal,
To see the buried ages all
Rise to answer at the call.

Now the books are open spread;
Now the writing must be read,
Which condemns the quick and dead:

Now, before the Judge severe
Hidden things must all appear;
Nought can pass unpunish’d here.

What shall guilty I then plead?
Who for me will intercede,
When the Saints shall comfort need?

King of dreadful Majesty!
Who dost freely justify!
Fount of Pity, save Thou me!

Recollect, O Love divine!
’Twas for this lost sheep of thine
Thou thy glory didst resign:

Satest wearied seeking me;
Sufferedst upon the Tree:
Let not vain thy labour be.

Judge of Justice, hear my prayer!
Spare me, Lord, in mercy spare!
Ere the Reckoning-day appear.

Lo! thy gracious face I seek;
Shame and grief are on my cheek;
Sighs and tears my sorrow speak.

Thou didst Mary’s guilt forgive;
Didst the dying thief receive;
Hence doth hope within me live.

Worthless are my prayers, I know;
Yet, oh, cause me not to go
Into everlasting woe.

Sever’d from the guilty band,
Make me with thy sheep to stand,
Placing me on thy right hand.

When the curs’d in anguish flee
Into flames of misery;
With the Blest then call Thou me.

Suppliant in the dust I lie;
My heart a cinder, crush’d and dry;
Help me, Lord, when death is nigh!

Full of tears, and full of dread,
Is the day that wakes the dead,
Calling all, with solemn blast,
From the ashes of the past.

Lord of mercy! Jesu blest!
Grant the Faithful light and rest.

translations.text:
Day of Wrath! O day of mourning!
See fulfill’d the prophets’ warning!
Heav’n and earth in ashes burning!
Oh, what fear man’s bosom rendeth
When from Heav’n the Judge descendeth,
On Whose sentence all dependeth!

Wondrous sound the trumpet flingeth,
Through earth’s sepulchres it ringeth,
All before the Throne it bringeth.
Death is struck, and nature quaking,
All creation is awaking,
To its Judge an answer making.

Lo! the Book exactly worded,
Wherein all hath been recorded;
Thence shall judgment be awarded.
When the Judge His seat attaineth,
And each hidden deed arraigneth,
Nothing unavenged remaineth.

What shall I, frail man, be pleading,
Who for me be interceding,
When the just are mercy needing?
King of Majesty tremendous,
Who dost free salvation send us,
Fount of pity, then befriend us!

Think, good Jesu, my salvation
Caused Thy wondrous Incarnation;
Leave me not to reprobation.
Faint and weary Thou hast sought me,
On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me?

Righteous Judge! for sin’s pollution
Grant Thy gift of absolution,
Ere that day of retribution.
Guilty, now I pour my moaning,
All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant groaning.

Thou the sinful woman savedst;
Thou the dying thief forgavest;
And to me a hope vouchsafest.
Worthless are my prayers and sighing;
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
Rescue me from fires undying.

With Thy favour’d sheep O place me,
Nor among the goats abase me,
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
While the wicked are confounded,
Doom’d to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me with Thy Saints surrounded.

Low I kneel, with heart submission,
See, like ashes, my contrition;
Help me in my last condition.

Ah! that day of tears and mourning!
From the dust of earth returning
Man for judgment must prepare him:
Spare, O God, in mercy spare him!
Lord, all-pitying, Jesu Blest,
Grant them Thine eternal rest.
Amen.

Who dost free salvation send us,

Caused Thy wondrous Incarnation;

On the Cross of suffering bought me;
Shall such grace be vainly brought me?

Ere that day of retribution.

All my shame with anguish owning;
Spare, O God, Thy suppliant groaning.

Thou the sinful woman savedst;
Thou the dying thief forgavest;
And to me a hope vouchsafest.
Worthless are my prayers and sighing;
Yet, good Lord, in grace complying,
Rescue me from fires undying.

With Thy favour’d sheep O place me,
Nor among the goats abase me,
But to Thy right hand upraise me.
While the wicked are confounded,
Doom’d to flames of woe unbounded,
Call me with Thy Saints surrounded.

See, like ashes, my contrition;
Help me in my last condition.

From the dust of earth returning
Man for judgment must prepare him:
Spare, O God, in mercy spare him!

Grant them Thine eternal rest.

translations.text:
Nigher still, and still more nigh
Draws the Day of Prophecy,
Doom’d to melt the earth and sky.

Oh, what trembling there shall be,
When the world its Judge shall see,
Coming in dread majesty!

Hark! the trump, with thrilling tone,
From sepulchral regions lone,
Summons all before the throne:

Time and Death it doth appal,
To see the buried ages all
Rise to answer at the call.

Now the books are open spread;
Now the writing must be read,
Which condemns the quick and dead:

Now, before the Judge severe
Hidden things must all appear;
Nought can pass unpunish’d here.

What shall guilty I then plead?
Who for me will intercede,
When the Saints shall comfort need?

King of dreadful Majesty!
Who dost freely justify!
Fount of Pity, save Thou me!

Recollect, O Love divine!
’Twas for this lost sheep of thine
Thou thy glory didst resign:

Satest wearied seeking me;
Sufferedst upon the Tree:
Let not vain thy labour be.

Judge of Justice, hear my prayer!
Spare me, Lord, in mercy spare!
Ere the Reckoning-day appear.

Lo! thy gracious face I seek;
Shame and grief are on my cheek;
Sighs and tears my sorrow speak.

Thou didst Mary’s guilt forgive;
Didst the dying thief receive;
Hence doth hope within me live.

Worthless are my prayers, I know;
Yet, oh, cause me not to go
Into everlasting woe.

Sever’d from the guilty band,
Make me with thy sheep to stand,
Placing me on thy right hand.

When the curs’d in anguish flee
Into flames of misery;
With the Blest then call Thou me.

Suppliant in the dust I lie;
My heart a cinder, crush’d and dry;
Help me, Lord, when death is nigh!

Full of tears, and full of dread,
Is the day that wakes the dead,
Calling all, with solemn blast,
From the ashes of the past.

Lord of mercy! Jesu blest!
Grant the Faithful light and rest.

A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

The 1861 keeps this feast on the Second Sunday after Epiphany, not on the Sunday between 2 and 5 January as the 1962 does. Leaf n104, printed p. 94, heads it `II. SUNDAY after EPIPHANY. The FEAST of the HOLY NAME JESUS.` over the Introit `In nomine Jesu`, and its Kalendar at leaf n774, printed p. 766, prints `Second Sunday after Epiphany- Feast of the most Holy Name of Jesus, d. of II. class 94`. The formulary is the same one, and the Latin cue set before this English is `Deus qui`, which answers the 1962's `Deus, qui Unigenitum`. The day placement is a recension difference and not a difference of text. Page-image collation confirms that this historical English body answers the complete target Latin identity; publication is limited to the 1861 wording and does not claim that Cummiskey appoints the 1962 celebration.

translations.text: O God, who didst appoint thy only begotten Son the Saviour of mankind, and commandest that his name should be called JESUS: mercifully grant, that we who venerate his holy name on earth, may also enjoy his sight in heaven. Thro'.

ordinary_frame.basis: This row withholds the whole bundled Palm Sunday entry because its blessing and procession are known to be the reformed service, while the boundary around the following Mass has not been collated or represented. Applying the ordinary frame to this unavailable bundle would present the 1861 Ordinary as though the withheld pre-1955 bundle had been established. The structural difference and its pre-1955 loci are recorded at roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml under `palmis.benedictio.*` and `palmis.distributio.*`.

also.basis: The 1962 book heads the day Dominica II Passionis seu in Palmis, and that title is the reform's own: Maxima Redemptionis fixes it in the sentence that says when the new Order begins, `Novus hic Ordo servari debet a die 25 Martii, dominica II Passionis seu in palmis, anni 1956` [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, departure maxima-redemptionis-1955/renamed, act cited at aas-47-1955 51853-51854]. The pre-1955 witnesses head it Dominica in Palmis [same file, mass dominica-in-palmis, attested by pustet-1862 28094 and missale-romanum-later-composite-pre-1955-body 31875-31877].

The Gospel of the entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 21, 1-9, is the same text in a different place in the service. The pre-1955 books read it BEFORE the blessing prayers [missale-romanum-later-composite-pre-1955-body 32017-32022, pustet-1862 28242-28247]; the 1962 book reads it AFTER the distribution of palms, under its own heading [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, unit palmis.benedictio.evangelium]. Neither book is missing it, which is why this is `reslotted` and not `absent` — the case the vocabulary was extended to name.

recension.basis: The inherited entry includes the reformed blessing and procession of palms. The pre-1955 books instead print the fourteen-unit service recorded under `palmis.benedictio.*` and `palmis.distributio.*`, while eleven of those units are absent from the 1962 witness [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml]. The Mass formulary after the procession has not been collated separately. Because the base bundles the known- different service with that Mass, serving the base entry would present reformed Holy Week material under a pre-1955 heading; this row therefore withholds the whole bundled entry until the boundary can be represented.

recension.basis: Maxima Redemptionis moved the Mass of the Lord's Supper to the evening; section 7 of the decree carries the provision [aas-47-1955 51905-51908, recorded at roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, departure maxima-redemptionis-1955/moved, mass feria-v-in-coena-domini]. The hour the pre-1955 books appoint is NOT ESTABLISHED: the act history's own mass row records `hour = "not established"` for this liturgy, where it fixes an hour for the other three. It is recorded moved because the decree says it moved, and the origin is left unstated rather than inferred from the general rubric on the hours of Mass.

ordinary_frame.basis: Feria VI in Parasceve is the exceptional Good Friday service, not a Mass formulary to be seated in the Ordinary transcribed from the 1861 lay missal. Its pre-1955 identity and hour were read at missale-romanum-later-composite-pre-1955-body 35401-35408 and pustet-1862 31916, and its known unit-level differences are recorded at roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml under `parasceve.*`.

also.basis: The pre-1955 books celebrate the liturgy of Good Friday in the morning, in choir after None [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, mass feria-vi-in-parasceve, attested by pustet-1862 31916 and missale-romanum-later-composite-pre-1955-body 35401-35403 with the hour at 35408]. Maxima Redemptionis moved it to the afternoon in terms: `Feria VI in Passione et Morte Domini solemnis actio liturgica celebratur horis postmeridianis` [aas-47-1955 51910-51911].

The same sentence renames the day. The pre-1955 heading is Feria VI in Parasceve; the reformed books head it Feria VI in Passione et Morte Domini and print that title in their running heads [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, departure maxima-redemptionis-1955/renamed].

The solemn prayer for the Jews differs between the witnesses in its invitatory, its rubric and its oration, and NO ACT FOR THE CHANGE WAS FOUND. The act history records all three as `unrecorded` and refuses to attach them to the 1962 edition merely because that is the first witness in which the words are gone [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, departures editio-typica-1962/unrecorded, units parasceve.orationes.pro-iudaeis-*]. It is carried here rather than dropped so that a page serving pre-1955 Good Friday cannot claim the base's text was checked for these units.

recension.basis: The solemn prayer for the Jews differs in its invitatory, rubric and oration between the pre-1955 witnesses and the inherited 1962 entry [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, units parasceve.orationes.pro-iudaeis-*]. The correspondence of the complete service has not been established. Serving the inherited formulary would therefore present known-different words under the pre-1955 heading, so this row serves no formulary wording.

ordinary_frame.basis: The pre-1955 Holy Saturday bundle has twelve prophecies, a Mass with no Postcommunion, and Vespers where the reformed entry has another structure. None of that pre-1955 wording is transcribed here, and the service has not been separated into a frame that can safely borrow the 1861 Ordinary. The established structure and witness loci are recorded at roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml under `sabbato.prophetiae.01` through `.12`, `sabbato.missa.*`, and `sabbato.vesperae.*`.

also.basis: The largest single departure in this file. The pre-1955 service is held on Saturday MORNING: it begins `Dicta Nona in Choro`, and the general rubric De hora celebrandi Missam allows Mass only `ab aurora usque ad meridiem` [missale-romanum-later-composite-pre-1955-body 37276 and 9614-9615, pustet-1862 33479 and 8151-8152; recorded at roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, mass sabbato-sancto, with the reasoning for the hour set out in `hour_basis` because no rubric in either witness fixes an hour in words]. Section 9 of Maxima Redemptionis moved it to the night, and the act history calls the evidence for this its strongest single piece: the decree's sentence at aas-47-1955 51915-51921 is reproduced WORD FOR WORD in the 1962 witness at benziger-iuxta-typicam-1962 40203-40212.

The day keeps its name and the liturgy within it is renamed: the decree speaks of the `solemnis paschalis vigilia` [aas-47-1955 51915] and the reformed book prints SABBATO SANCTO with DE VIGILIA PASCHALI beneath it [benziger-iuxta-typicam-1962 40187, 40195].

The case this repository's recension model was built to carry, and the one that generated false absences before it existed. The pre-1955 Mass of Holy Saturday HAS NO POSTCOMMUNION — its own rubric suppresses one — and the office that follows is VESPERS, whose Oratio is the prayer Spiritum nobis. The reformed book suppresses no Postcommunion and prints one, and the office that follows is LAUDS of the Resurrection, with Benedictus for Magnificat and the antiphon Valde mane for Vespere autem sabbati [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, units sabbato.missa.rubrica-nec-postcommunio and sabbato.vesperae.*]. A matcher keyed on (mass, proper-name) asked the pre-1955 book for a slot the reform created, got nothing, and wrote down an absence; the words were on the page the whole time, in another slot.

recension.basis: The pre-1955 books print twelve prophecies where the reformed book prints four lessons, suppress a Postcommunion, and follow the Mass with Vespers rather than Lauds [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, units sabbato.prophetiae.01 through .12, sabbato.missa.* and sabbato.vesperae.*]. Those are known structural and textual differences, while no pre-1955 wording has been verified for service here. The inherited reformed Vigil is therefore replaced by a typed unavailable formulary state.

translations.text:
Forth to the paschal Victim, Christians, bring
Your sacrifice of praise:

The Lamb redeems the sheep;
And Christ, the Sinless One,
Hath to the Father sinners reconcil’d.

Together, Death and Life
In a strange conflict strove;
The Prince of Life, who died,
Now lives and reigns.

What thou sawest, Mary, say,
As thou wentest on the way.

I saw the tomb wherein the Living One had lain;
I saw his glory as He rose again;
Napkin and linen clothes, and Angels twain:
Yea, Christ is risen, my hope, and He
Will go before you into Galilee.

We know that Christ indeed has risen from the grave:
Hail, thou King of Victory!
Have mercy, Lord, and save.

translations.text:
Forth to the paschal Victim, Christians, bring
Your sacrifice of praise:

The Lamb redeems the sheep;
And Christ, the Sinless One,
Hath to the Father sinners reconcil’d.

Together, Death and Life
In a strange conflict strove;
The Prince of Life, who died,
Now lives and reigns.

What thou sawest, Mary, say,
As thou wentest on the way.

I saw the tomb wherein the Living One had lain;
I saw his glory as He rose again;
Napkin and linen clothes, and Angels twain:
Yea, Christ is risen, my hope, and He
Will go before you into Galilee.

We know that Christ indeed has risen from the grave:
Hail, thou King of Victory!
Have mercy, Lord, and save.

translations.text:
Sion, lift thy voice, and sing;
Praise thy Saviour and thy King;
Praise with hymns thy Shepherd true:
Strive thy best to praise Him well;
Yet doth He all praise excel;
None can ever reach His due.

See to-day before us laid
The living and life-giving Bread!
Theme for praise and joy profound!
The same which at the sacred board
Was, by our Incarnate Lord,
Giv’n to his Apostles round.

Let the praise be loud and high;
Sweet and tranquil be the joy
Felt to-day in every breast;
On this Festival divine,
Which records the origin
Of the glorious Eucharist.

On this Table of the King,
Our new Paschal offering
Brings to end the olden rite;
Here, for empty shadows fled,
Is Reality instead;
Here, instead of darkness, Light.

His own act, at supper seated,
Christ ordain’d to be repeated,
In His Memory divine;
Wherefore now, with adoration,
We the Host of our salvation
Consecrate from bread and wine.

Hear what holy Church maintaineth,
That the bread its substance changeth
Into Flesh, the wine to Blood.
Doth it pass thy comprehending?
Faith, the law of sight transcending,
Leaps to things not understood.

Here, beneath these signs, are hidden
Priceless things, to sense forbidden;
Signs, not things, are all we see;—
Flesh from bread, and Blood from wine;
Yet is Christ, in either sign,
All entire, confess’d to be.

They too, who of Him partake,
Sever not, nor rend, nor break,
But entire, their Lord receive.
Whether one or thousands eat,
All receive the self-same meat,
Nor the less for others leave.

Both the wicked and the good
Eat of this celestial Food;
But with ends how opposite!
Here ’tis life; and there ’tis death;
The same, yet issuing to each
In a difference infinite.

Nor a single doubt retain,
When they break the Host in twain,
But that in each part remains
What was in the whole before;
Since the simple sign alone
Suffers change in state or form,
The Signified remaining One
And the Same for evermore.

Lo! upon the Altar lies,
Hidden deep from human eyes,
Bread of Angels from the skies,
Made the food of mortal man:
Children’s meat to dogs denied;
In old types foresignified;
In the manna Heav’n-supplied,
Isaac, and the Paschal Lamb.

Jesu! Shepherd of the sheep!
Thou thy flock in safety keep.
Living Bread! thy life supply;
Strengthen us, or else we die;
Fill us with celestial grace:
Thou, who feedest us below!
Source of all we have or know!
Grant that with thy Saints above,
Sitting at the feast of love,
We may see Thee face to face.

ordinary_frame.basis: This is the blessing and distribution of palms which precedes the Mass, not a Mass formulary to be seated in the Ordo Missae. Its fourteen units, including its own Preface and Sanctus, are recorded from the 1862 witness and the later composite's 1951-1954 body at roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml under `palmis.benedictio.*` and `palmis.distributio.*`.

recension.basis: The pre-1955 blessing of palms is a service of fourteen units the 1962 book does not print, and it is `added` rather than a difference within Palm Sunday because the base holds no entry for it at all. Eleven of the fourteen are recorded `absent` at the 1955 station with a per-unit basis [roman-holy-week-acts-v1.toml, units palmis.benedictio.* and palmis.distributio.*, each attested by pustet-1862 and missale-romanum-later-composite-pre-1955-body with loci]. Among them are a Lectio from Exodus, a Graduale, a full Preface and Sanctus, and six orations; the 1962 blessing runs from the antiphon straight to a single blessing prayer.

blockers.requirement: Register and fingerprint one complete page-image artifact of the 1920 Vatican typical edition before its wording or page loci become corpus evidence.
Transcribe and page-collate the target edition's calendar, Propers, Commons, Ordinary, and Holy Week. OCR may locate text but may not supply it; the measured correction rate was 38 of 99 orations.
Give every Proper a per-witness attestation before residence is moved from roman-1962 or inherited text is described as pre-1955.
Read a pre-1955 general calendar from page images, including grades, octaves, and vigils; do not reconstruct it by subtracting 1962.

Model the five ordered criteria directly, including the different role of propriety in occurrence and concurrence, and replace the present numbered linearization with source-shaped evaluation and solved cases.
Locate the 1900 typical edition that the 1920 decree names as its parent, closing the act history's one `via_unrepresented` edge.
Read the restricted 1956 Ordo in a lawful accessible copy and model the 1956-1960 middle state before attributing every pre-1955-to-1962 Holy Week difference to the 1955 reform.
Keep the blessing of oils outside the Missal claim until an identified pre-1955 Pontificale Romanum edition is registered and read.

calendar.basis: Six Holy Week departures and two exact post-1954 sanctoral absences are stated. The remainder of the temporal and sanctoral calendar is inherited from roman-1962 without a pre-1955 kalendarium collation, including the octaves and vigils affected by the March 1955 simplification.

ceremonies.basis: The act history records structural units for Palm Sunday and the Triduum from OCR and promulgating acts. It expressly excludes a complete ceremonial, notation, the Office, and unstated units.

commons.basis: Every Common is inherited from roman-1962. No pre-1955 witness has been collated against those formularies, so inheritance proves availability in the projection and not identity in the target recension.

ordinary.basis: A separate Ordinary inventory transcribes the 1861 Cummiskey lay missal, including its facing Latin where printed. It is neither the 1920 altar book nor an element-by-element collation against that typical edition.

precedence.basis: The companion rubrics source openly linearizes the five Divino afflatu criteria into numbered rows. It records divergences and supports a finding aid, but it does not implement the criteria as criteria.

propers.basis: No Proper wording in this departure file is transcribed from or page-collated against the 1920 typical edition. Known-different bundled formularies carry typed unavailable status and no pseudo-Proper rows; unstated formularies are mechanical roman-1962 fallback, not pre-1955 attestations.

evidence.basis: The inventory records the unit-level structure and acts behind these Holy Week departures, while refusing its OCR readings as witnesses to wording. Its source formerly labelled as the 1920 printing is a later composite, body 1951-1954 with a post-1970 appendix; that OCR is held only as a structural/search witness and does not establish exact target-edition correspondence.
Titulus II of the 1911 rubrics was read in the publisher PDF. The current table is a disclosed linearization of its five criteria rather than a claim that the source printed numbered precedence rows.
The 1861 witness was transcribed from page images at the grades its inventory states. This establishes that witness only, not the wording of the 1920 typical edition.

`[the_1920_substitution.where_it_cannot]`, item 3, and `[the_1920_substitution.a_defect_in_the_1920_artifact_itself].finding` record the separately verified absence of the Queenship of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St Joseph the Worker from the pre-reform witness body. The artifact record bounds that body to 1951-1954, records zero `Opific` hits, and records `Reginae` only in old local-indult material. The same inventory item's St Pius X negative was corrected as false, so these rows rely only on the two retained and reverified results and make no claim about St Pius X.

inheritance.basis: `text_from` is a mechanical fallback to the only target altar-book corpus transcribed in this repository. It does not assert that any unstated 1962 entry was checked in a pre-1955 witness or remained unchanged.

THIS IS HYMNS ANCIENT AND MODERN'S TEXT OF IRONS AND NOT DEMONSTRABLY IRONS'S
OWN. That book's compilers are widely said to have altered what they received;

of the transcription.
